message.content:
reacquaint and I'm talking to web-claude and asked if criterion is determining the
benchmark overhead by, it says yes but not by using a calibration phase and
calculating ad overhead figure, instead it says:
"Criterion runs your benchmarked closure across a range of iteration counts
(batch sizes) and records (iterations, elapsed_time) pairs for each sample.
It then does an ordinary least-squares linear regression on those pairs. The
slope of that regression line is what it reports as "time per iteration."

It seems to be the noise is so high is that technique worth it?

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. # Todo

This file uses [Prose form](AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

_No cycle currently in progress._

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run TODO.md` to renumber.
The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
number. Long-tail entries
live in [todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the
[Prose Form in AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper
detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. Drop overhead adjustment; grade the run from raw batches —
   the 0.23.0 cycle, decided in
   [Replanning II](notes/chores/chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run)
   - remove startup calibration, the constants block, adjusted
     columns, and the `calibrate` command; raw values only,
     one README sentence on apparatus framing
   - `pick_inner` sizing from a ~1 ms micro-probe (low
     quantile over back-to-back timer pairs), never printed
   - per-run quality gauge computed at the end from the run's
     own data: samples land in raw time-ordered batches,
     per-batch summaries (floor, mean, census counts) feed the
     gauge, then bulk-record into the histogram; relocate the
     -5 grade machinery (signals, thresholds, letter, warnings)
   - absorbs the interference-crossover entry's rate analysis
     (below) — batches give it the time axis
   - the overhead.rs deletion largely replaces the planned
     acquisition/estimation refactor
2. Guard `--pin` pools smaller than the bench's thread
   placements, and deadline the estimate phase — `zcr-mpsc-2t
   --pin 8` put both spinning software threads on one logical
   CPU and appeared hung until ^C (2026-07-26, bug #1 in
   [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md#bugs))
   - track `core_for` requests in `RunCfg` (max `thread_idx`
     asked for); refuse the run when placements exceed unique
     CPUs in the pool — placement only goes through `core_for`
     when pinning is active, so the guard covers every path,
     and no pinning means the scheduler separates the spinners
     itself

1180	### Replanning II: drop the adjustment, grade the run
1181	
1182	Recorded 2026-07-26, after -5's first cross-machine outing.
1183	Three findings converged into a philosophy change: the
1184	remaining rungs (-6 warmup-until-stable, -7 report only what
1185	is applied) are retired, the cycle closes after -5, and the
1186	redesign is the "Drop overhead adjustment" Todo (the next
1187	cycle).
1188	
1189	**The r5-7600x F.** A demonstrably quiet r5-7600x graded F
1190	while the visibly busy 3900X got D. The self-checks read the
1191	mechanism correctly — drift bracket `l_start` 42.750 ->
1192	`l_end` 38.051 ns/sample, 11% *faster* (interference only
1193	slows; getting faster is a clock ramp); the ladder's per-iter
1194	falls monotonically 0.4275 -> 0.3680; the 12.7% slope cross
1195	and 12.5% repeat are the same event seen twice; meanwhile
1196	disturbed 0.07% and `frame/sample` 8.310 ns, dead on that

content.text:
Reacquainted — 0.22.0 published yesterday; two uncommitted notes edits (chores-04 `Commits:` backfill, cycle-protocol lesson on the empty-commit push mishap); no cycle in progress; Todo #1 is the 0.23.0 raw-batches redesign.

On the Criterion question: web-claude's description is accurate. Criterion's linear sampling mode times the closure at iteration counts `d, 2d, 3d, … Nd`, then fits OLS on the (iterations, elapsed) pairs and reports the slope. And notably, we already ran this exact experiment ourselves — the 0.22.0-4 rung ("slope from multi-N loop-only passes") *is* this technique, so we have direct evidence on how it behaves under our noise.

What the regression actually buys:

- The **intercept absorbs fixed per-sample overhead** — the timer reads and sample setup that happen once per sample regardless of N. That's the quantity our `frame/sample` calibration chased, and the regression removes it without a separate calibration phase or any subtraction, because it's estimated on the same data it's applied to. No transferability problem — this is the genuinely sound part, and it's why Criterion can report sub-nanosecond operations at all, where per-sample framing would otherwise dominate.
- The **slope still contains per-iteration overhead** (loop counter, the call into the closure, `black_box`). Criterion doesn't remove that any more than our raw numbers do. So it removes less than people usually assume.

Is it worth it under high noise? Mostly no, and for a structural reason: the regression sorts noise by whether it scales with N. Fixed per-sample noise lands harmlessly in the intercept — but the noise that actually hurt us is **time-proportional and one-sided** (preemption probability grows with elapsed time, interference only ever adds). That noise scales with N, so it lands directly in the slope, and OLS gives the largest-N samples — the longest ones, most likely to catch a preemption — the most leverage. So the regression defends against the component that cancels in A/B comparison anyway, and is defenseless against the component that doesn't. Our own -4/-5 data showed the outcome: the slope repeated precisely within a run but swung ~10% between runs with frequency regime — precision without accuracy, which is what drove Replanning II. (Criterion partially compensates with big sample counts, bootstrap CIs, and reporting median/MAD alongside the slope — but the headline number is still the OLS slope.)

So the verdict splits by purpose. For Criterion's purpose — one-shot absolute timing of arbitrary closures, including sub-ns ones, on machines it can't characterize — the regression is a reasonable engineering trade and better than a calibrate-then-subtract design (which we proved fragile). For this project's purpose — A/B on one harness, where the fixed framing is common-mode — it buys nothing the raw numbers don't already have, and the batch-pipeline gauge in Todo #1 addresses the time-proportional noise that regression structurally cannot.

The plain version: Criterion's trick automatically cancels the fixed cost of starting and stopping the stopwatch, which is clever and works. But the noise that plagued us isn't stopwatch cost — it's the machine randomly slowing down mid-measurement, and that gets baked into Criterion's answer just like it gets baked into ours. Since we only compare runs against each other on the same rig, the stopwatch cost cancels for free anyway, so the trick solves a problem we don't have and skips the one we do.

content.text:
The bug claim checks out, and verifying it surfaced something bigger that corrects my previous answer. Three things:

**The R² bug is real.** In `src/stats/bivariate/regression.rs`, on both master and the 0.5.1 release, the loop reads `ss_tot = ss_res + (y - y_bar).powi(2)` — assignment onto the current `ss_res`, not accumulation onto `ss_tot`. The final `ss_tot` is just the last iteration's residual sum plus one squared deviation, so the reported R² is meaningless. Web-claude is also right that the slope is unaffected (it's computed separately in `fit`). Conclusion: don't lean on Criterion's goodness-of-fit output.

**Criterion's regression has no intercept — I was wrong about that last turn.** The same file shows `Slope::fit` computes `xy / x2`: a through-origin fit, `y = m·x`. So my claim that "the intercept absorbs fixed per-sample overhead" was wrong — there is no intercept, and Criterion does *not* remove per-sample framing at all; it gets folded into the slope (small at large N, but a real upward bias). That makes web-claude's phrasing exactly right: an intercept fit would put you *ahead of* Criterion, not equal to it. It also weakens the case I made for Criterion's technique — the one genuinely sound thing I credited it with, it doesn't actually do.

**On the recommendation itself, I'd still let Replanning II stand.** The in-run intercept fit does fix the objection it targets — estimating overhead on the same data it's applied to kills the transferability problem, which is real progress over our startup calibration. But it answers only one of Replanning II's four objections. The others are untouched: additivity is itself an approximation on a superscalar CPU; the correction is ~1.5 ns with uncertainty a good fraction of itself; and for A/B on one harness the framing is common-mode and cancels unsubtracted. And the noise structure from last turn still applies — one-sided, time-proportional contamination lands in the *slope*, and because OLS with an intercept estimates slope and intercept jointly, a few contaminated high-N samples move both. That last point undercuts the canary idea specifically: intercept instability would confound frequency-regime shifts with ordinary interference, whereas the batch pipeline's floor-over-time series gives the same boost/thermal signal cleanly, with time resolution, and it's already the 0.23.0 design. There's also a mechanical cost the advice glosses over: an in-run regression needs multiple iteration counts per run, which cuts against the fixed `pick_inner` sizing and complicates the histogram (samples at different N have different variance and quantization).

So: adopt the skepticism about Criterion's R², enjoy the confirmation that an intercept fit would out-do Criterion, but I wouldn't reopen the drop decision. If the intercept-fit-as-instrument idea seems worth keeping, it fits naturally as a `## Ideas` entry ("revisitable, nothing forecloses it" — the config-file opt-in note in Replanning II already holds the door open); say the word and I'll add it.

The plain version: the bug is genuinely there — Criterion's "how well does the line fit" number is computed wrong, though its main timing number is fine. I also discovered Criterion's line is forced through zero, so it never separates out the fixed measurement cost — meaning the fancier version web-claude proposes really would be better than Criterion. But better than Criterion isn't the bar; our plan already sidesteps the whole problem by comparing raw numbers on the same rig, and the redesign we have queued watches for the machine warming up or slowing down more directly than the proposed canary would.

content.text:
Confirmed first: the successor repo (`criterion-rs/criterion.rs`) has the identical bug at the same line — `ss_tot = ss_res + (y - y_bar).powi(2)` — so web-claude is right; the fork carried it forward.

On the idea: I think it's good, but it splits into two different regressions, and only one of them earns its keep. The conflation is easy to make because both are "OLS over the run's data."

**Regression against time (batch index) — yes, adopt it.** This is Criterion's *machinery* pointed at our *question*. The batch pipeline in Todo #1 already produces the input: per-batch floors and means in time order. Fit a line to batch floor vs. time and the slope *is* the drift measurement — the drift-bracket signal from -5, but as a proper fit over the whole run instead of two endpoints, with residuals localizing bursts ("interference clustered at ~3.2 s") and a correctly-computed R² as a stability figure. This fits "grade the exam, not the room" exactly: it's computed at the end, from the run's own recorded data, never subtracted from anything. It also answers the canary desire from web-claude's advice with a cleaner instrument — floor-vs-time slope tracks boost/thermal state directly, with time resolution, no intercept confound. One refinement given our one-sided noise: fit the *floors* (or use a robust estimator like Theil–Sen) rather than OLS on means, so bursts show up in residuals and census counts instead of dragging the trend line.

**Regression against iteration count (Criterion's actual axis) — no, don't reshape acquisition for it.** Getting a slope-vs-N fit requires deliberately varying the inner-loop N across samples during the run. That costs real things: `pick_inner`'s fixed sizing goes away, samples at different N have different variance and quantization so the histogram becomes a mixture, and per-sample codegen/cache behavior shifts with N — the exact class of trouble the 0.22 cycle spent five rungs fighting. And we already know what it yields on our hardware: the -4 multi-N slope was precise but not accurate (10% run-to-run swing with frequency regime), and the 3900X's ~9% ladder bend says the linear model itself doesn't hold well across N there. As a *grading* signal that bend is thin evidence from one machine; not enough to justify restructuring acquisition.

So the recast I'd propose for Todo #1: the quality gauge's drift and burst signals become a regression over the time-ordered batch summaries — which is an enrichment of the existing bullet, not a new direction. The frame/intercept decomposition stays dropped from the default path; if you ever want it back as a reported-only diagnostic, it's a small opt-in probe and belongs in `## Ideas`. Happy to fold that wording into the Todo #1 entry if you want it recorded.

The plain version: yes to borrowing the fit-a-line trick, but point it at a different axis. Criterion fits time against how-many-iterations to untangle overhead — that axis forced us to change how we collect data, and it burned us. Fitting against when-during-the-run instead tells us whether the machine sped up, slowed down, or got interrupted mid-run — which is precisely what a grade should measure — and our planned batch design already collects exactly the data that line needs.

message.content: I'm wondering if we should use a small set of initial runs and or final runs that does that iteration count regression, especially when runs are short and inner is > 1. Would that be useful for quality control when used along side of the time regression?

content.text:
Good instinct — and it's worth noticing that this proposal is very close to machinery we already built: the 0.22.0-4/-5 "multi-N loop-only passes" plus the `l_start`/`l_end` drift bracket *are* an N-sweep bracket at the run's edges. Replanning II retired them as *calibration* (produce a constant, subtract it). What you're proposing is keeping them as *instrumentation* (produce a QC signal, report it) — and that reframing dodges most of what killed them. So: yes, useful, under specific design constraints.

What the brackets add that the time regression can't:

- **Decomposition.** With fixed inner N, a batch-floor shift on the time axis is ambiguous — per-sample frame change or per-iteration change, you can't tell; with inner > 1 the frame is amortized and nearly invisible in the samples. An N-sweep gives slope and intercept separately, so start-vs-end comparison says *which* moved. Frequency ramps move per-iteration time; a frame shift with a stable slope points at something else. That's a diagnostic dimension the time axis simply doesn't have.
- **Coverage for short runs.** Exactly your case: a short run yields few batches, so the floor-vs-time fit is underpowered right when ramp contamination is most likely. The brackets don't shrink with run length.
- **The ramp detector.** The r5-7600x F taught us that a startup probe on a deep-idle box measures the ramp itself. As a *grade of the machine* that was wrong; as a start-vs-end disagreement flag it's precisely right — "this run began in a different frequency regime than it ended" is the single most useful warning a short run can carry.

The design constraints that keep it from re-becoming calibration:

- **Differential only.** Compare start bracket to end bracket, and run to run — never use either as an absolute number, never subtract anything. Differential use also cancels the model error we measured: the 3900X's ~9% ladder bend sits in both brackets of the same run, so it mostly drops out of the comparison. Absolute use is where the 10% regime swing bit us; differential use is robust to it.
- **Robust per-N points.** Floor (or low quantile) per N step, not means — the 0.22 pairing-discipline lesson, since one preemption in a ~ms bracket would otherwise fake a regime shift.
- **Outside the measured run.** Brackets don't touch acquisition: `pick_inner`'s fixed sizing stays, the histogram never sees bracket samples. This preserves my prior objection's target — it was varying N *within* the run that was bad.
- **Tiny output surface.** Two or three gauge signals (bracket slope shift %, intercept shift %, maybe per-bracket fit residual) feeding the letter grade — not a constants block. The scope-creep risk here is real; the moment a bracket number gets printed as "overhead," we're back where Replanning II started.

Alongside the time regression the roles split cleanly: batch-floor-vs-time watches the run's interior (drift trend, burst localization); the brackets watch the edges and decompose what the interior fit can only detect. The end bracket is the more trustworthy of the two (machine warm); the start bracket's job is mostly to disagree with it when the run started cold.

Net: I'd fold this into Todo #1 as a refinement — the -5 grade machinery relocates onto run data *and* the -4/-5 ladder+bracket code survives as the edge instrument, differential-only. Want me to update the Todo #1 entry to capture both this and the time-regression recast from last turn?

The plain version: run a tiny stopwatch self-test just before and just after the real measurement, and compare the two — never trust either alone, only the difference. If they disagree, the machine changed speed during the run, which is exactly when a short run's numbers deserve a warning label. It complements the trend line we fit through the run itself: the trend line watches the middle, the self-tests guard the two ends, and neither one ever adjusts the reported numbers — they only grade them.

content.text:
Your recollection is right: the run harness warms up with a fixed `WARMUP: u64 = 10_000` steps (`src/harness.rs:11,183`), after which `estimate_step_cost` and `pick_inner` run immediately. (There's also `BLOCK_WARMUP_SECONDS = 0.002` per block in blocked mode, and calibration's separate `CAL_WARMUP = 100_000` — but that one dies with overhead.rs in 0.23.0.)

Yes, it should be dynamic — and the fixed *count* is the worst of the options, for a reason we've already measured. A count-based warmup's wall-clock duration scales with step cost: a ~1 ns bench gets ~10 µs of warmup, a ~1 µs bench gets ~10 ms. Frequency-governor ramps live at tens-to-hundreds of ms — the r5-7600x diagnosis. So the fastest benches, where per-sample numbers are most ramp-sensitive, get the *least* warmup in the only unit that matters to the governor, and `pick_inner`'s sizing probe runs mid-ramp on exactly those benches. A fixed *time* (say 200 ms of stepping) would at least be governor-scale, but it taxes every run on already-warm boxes — the 7600X-with-performance-governor case pays for the deep-idle case's problem.

The right shape is the retired -6 design, warm-until-stable: probe repeatedly until consecutive readings agree, with a hard cap. Replanning II mooted it *as calibration warmup* — but the run-warmup problem it solved never went away, and your question is the correct place for it to resurface. What makes it especially attractive now is that it fuses with the bracket idea from last turn:

- Warm by running short floor probes (or mini N-sweeps) back to back; terminate when two consecutive ones agree within tolerance, capped at some governor-scale maximum (a few hundred ms).
- The final probe — the one that demonstrated stability — **is the start bracket**. No separate instrument, no double cost; warmup termination and the start-bracket measurement are the same act.
- On a warm box (performance governor, mid-session) it exits almost immediately — near-zero tax. On a deep-idle box it runs as long as the ramp does, which is precisely the adaptive behavior a fixed anything can't give.
- Hitting the cap without stabilizing is itself a gauge signal: "run started unstable" — the machine never settled, and the grade should say so rather than the warmup pretending it did. That converts the failure mode into information instead of a silent bad run.

The costs are two new thresholds (agreement tolerance, cap) — constants of the kind this project has learned to distrust, so they'd want the same loud-fail treatment as the -5 thresholds — and floors-not-means in the probes so one preemption doesn't fake stability or instability. `pick_inner` then runs after stability, which also retroactively firms up the micro-probe's readings. The per-block 2 ms warmup is a separate, milder question (post-sleep re-ramp is also governor-scale, so it's likely short) — but blocked mode deliberately re-rolls machine state, so I'd leave it alone until the batch pipeline's per-batch floors can actually show us what post-wake recovery looks like.

This is now three connected refinements to Todo #1 (time-axis regression, differential brackets, warm-until-stable fused with the start bracket) — worth landing in the entry as a coherent update rather than carrying in conversation. Want me to rewrite Todo #1 to fold them in?

The plain version: today the warmup runs a fixed number of repetitions, so fast operations finish warming in microseconds — long before the CPU has actually sped up to full clock. Better to keep warming until the measurements themselves stop changing, then stop: a warm machine costs almost nothing, a cold machine gets exactly the time it needs, and if it never settles, that fact goes into the run's grade instead of being hidden.

content.text:
2-in-a-row can indeed be an accident, and you're not wrong — there's even a mechanism-specific reason it's worse than generic noise would suggest. Frequency governors climb through discrete P-states, and a dwell at an intermediate state is exactly two-probes-shaped: readings plateau for a beat, then step again. Two consecutive floors agreeing can certify a ledge on the staircase, not the top. (One-sided noise is the *lesser* risk here — floors are robust against upward contamination; the stepwise ramp is the real spoofer, and it's the very ladder shape 0.22 kept meeting.) Three consecutive agreements require the plateau to outlast two full probe intervals, which most dwells won't; and since each probe is ~1 ms, demanding 3–4 costs single-digit milliseconds on a warm box — trivial insurance. I'd spec it as a small constant defaulting to 3, with 5 as the paranoid end; past that you're buying little and delaying cap-detection of a genuinely unstable box.

message.content: Seems to me that our dynamic warm-up should be part of the pick_inner and we kill two birds with one stone?

content.text:
Yes — and it's better than two-birds convenience; the fusion fixes a subtle defect in the separated design. The strongest version of it: make the warmup probe *be* the sizing probe, repeated until it converges.

The reasoning:

- The quantity `pick_inner` needs (step-cost floor, plus the timer-frame micro-probe) is exactly the quantity whose stability we care about. So "warm until stable" naturally becomes "repeat the sizing probe until K consecutive floors agree, and the final one *is* the sizing input." The convergence test runs on the very number we're about to consume — you can't certify stability on a proxy and then measure the real thing in a different regime, which is a residual risk of a separate warmup.
- It guarantees post-ramp sizing by construction. Today `estimate_step_cost` runs right after the fixed warmup, i.e. potentially mid-ramp — that's the actual bug behind mid-ramp `pick_inner` sizing. Fused, the sizing number can't exist until stability has been demonstrated, so the defect is structurally impossible rather than hopefully avoided.
- The probe load is the *bench's own* steps, so the warmup warms the right things — the bench's code path, caches, branch predictors — and generates the load that drives the governor up, not just timer-read spin.
- Bonus bird: the hard cap on the probe loop is very close to the "deadline the estimate phase" bullet in Todo #3 (the `--pin 8` livelock hang). One capped probe loop can serve both — a bench that never converges *and* a bench that's pathologically slow both hit the same deadline with a diagnostic, instead of hanging.

One thing the fusion quietly changes: the probe now measures step-cost floor at a single N, not an N-sweep — so the "start bracket" doubling loses the slope/intercept decomposition. I think that's fine and arguably cleaner: differential QC becomes "repeat the same probe at run end and compare floors" — same instrument, start vs. end, no acquisition of any second axis. The N-sweep decomposition stays an Ideas-tier option if the batch data ever shows we need to distinguish frame shifts from per-iteration shifts.

I'll fold this into the Todo #2 entry.

content.text:
Todo #2 now reads as the fused design: the warmup probe is the sizing probe repeated to convergence, K=3, floors only, one governor-scale cap serving both the stability exit and the estimate-phase deadline that the `--pin` guard entry wanted, and start-vs-end QC as a repeat of the same probe. Note that Todo #1's ~1 ms timer-pair micro-probe is untouched and still separate — it measures the *frame* input to `pick_inner`, while the fused probe loop supplies the *step-cost* input; the two are complementary, not duplicates.

The plain version: instead of warming up first and then measuring how big the inner loop should be, we measure repeatedly from the start and simply refuse to accept an answer until it stops changing. The warm-up, the loop sizing, and the "did this machine ever settle down" check all become one mechanism — and the sizing can no longer be taken while the CPU is still speeding up, because an unsettled measurement is by definition not yet an answer.

message.content: How will it handle situations where inner is small like 1?

content.text:
Short answer: `inner = 1` is the easy case for *sizing* but the awkward case for *probing* — and conveniently, the stakes fall exactly where the probing gets expensive.

Unpacking that:

- **The mechanism doesn't depend on `inner` at all.** The probe loop runs before sizing and measures raw step cost; `pick_inner` returning 1 just means the step is slow enough that framing is negligible. Convergence logic is unchanged. The real variable behind your question is *step cost*, because that's what sets how many steps fit in a probe.
- **Where it bites: a fixed ~1 ms probe starves.** At 25 µs/step (zcr-mpsc territory) a 1 ms probe holds ~40 steps — a floor over 40 is serviceable. At ms-scale steps it holds one or zero, and a "floor" of one sample is just a sample. So the probe must adapt: minimum step count *or* minimum wall time, whichever is larger — meaning probe duration grows with step cost, and K=3 probes of a slow bench can want ~1 s of warmup.
- **That collides with the cap, so the cap's exit must distinguish two causes.** Hitting the deadline because consecutive floors *disagreed* means "run started unstable" — a genuine gauge signal. Hitting it because steps are too slow to complete K adequate probes means "too slow to certify" — proceed, but label the run as uncertified rather than unstable. One deadline, two diagnostics; conflating them would hand slow benches a permanent false F, the r5-7600x mistake in a new costume.
- **Two effects soften the slow-step case.** First, slow probes span more wall time each, so consecutive agreement naturally covers governor timescales — the ramp-detection job partly does itself; the fast benches that need many probes are also the ones whose probes are cheap. Second, the harm being prevented shrinks: mid-ramp sizing error matters when `inner` is large and sensitive, but at `inner = 1` the sizing can't come out wrong (it's the minimum), and framing is noise against a µs-scale step. The residual value of warmup there is warming the bench's own path and giving the start-floor for end-of-run differential QC — worth having, not worth a second of stubborn probing, which argues for the "certify or proceed-with-label" exit rather than blocking.

I'll add that adaptation to the Todo #2 entry.

- #2's fused design presumes the post-#1 world. The warmup-pass loop replaces `estimate_step_cost` + fixed `WARMUP` *and* feeds `pick_inner`, whose frame input becomes #1's micro-probe (today it's `cfg.overhead.frame_call_ns` — a field of the very constants block #1 deletes). Building #2 on the current calibration-era harness means immediately rebuilding it when overhead.rs dies.
- #2's outputs need #1's receiver. "Run started unstable" / "uncertified" are gauge signals — the relocated grade machinery and batch pipeline are where they land. Without #1 there's nowhere to report but the doomed calibration-time grade.
- The reverse dependency doesn't exist: #1 can keep the fixed `WARMUP = 10_000` untouched and still deliver everything it promises. One imperfect constant surviving one cycle is fine — it's survived many.

On the pending doc changes: they slot naturally into the 0.23.0-0 prep commit rather than a separate notes-only push — the chores-04 `Commits:` backfill is *specified* to land with the next push, the cycle-protocol lesson is finished text, and the TODO.md edits are literally the cycle's planning. # Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running
artifact. The scheme — the cycle step-numbering and the
unique-per-commit aim — is generic and shared across projects:
this file is copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
covering each medium by conditional rather than per-project
edits.

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version** — the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`),
  written with `-` in prose, ladders, chores, todo, and commit
  talk; its suffix encodes the cycle phase (see
  [Step numbering](#step-numbering)).
- **version-of-record** — the authoritative stored copy of the
  version, in the project's manifest (see
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record));
  a built or running artifact derives from it.
- **versioning** — the topic: this scheme as a whole.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and
surfaced, and how often it changes — pick the case that fits
your medium:

- **Manifest** — where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the
    committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic
    `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter, …) — add the case as
    needed
- **Notation** — how the `-` form is stored:
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`),
    store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python
    project), remap to `+` — `0.3.0-5.3.0` → `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same
    version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter** — how a built artifact surfaces the
  version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence** — how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement);
  this project follows the per-commit preference.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change
on **every commit**, so a built or running artifact identifies
the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project
  following the cycle protocol may bump less often — once per
  cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
  if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are
  **pre-assignable**, unlike the git SHA, which a commit cannot
  contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

## Step numbering

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out; see
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes each commit's
phase in the version suffix — the **final identifier `0` marks
a Preparation**:

- `X.Y.Z-0` — Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, … — Work commits
- `X.Y.Z` — Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle — no ladder,
no setup commit — skips `-0` and starts at `-1` (its first
Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that
grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step without
renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10` — Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a
  Preparation.
- `-1.0` — Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final
  identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0` — Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2` — its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3` — its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0` — Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of each phase, so the
active phase is recorded — and, per the preference above,
every commit carries a distinct version.

1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
7	the conversation — code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
8	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
9	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
10	equivalents — this project's manifest is recorded in
11	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
12	
13	## Cycles
14	
15	A cycle has three phases:
16	
17	- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`) — the cycle's
18	  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
19	  it and starts at `-1` — see
20	  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
21	  cycle:
22	  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
23	    and the suffix scheme are project-specific — see
24	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
25	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
26	    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
27	    statement + plan ladder).
28	  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
29	- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) — the
30	  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
31	  needs; each runs through the
32	  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
33	- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`) — the cycle's
34	  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
35	  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
36	    `## Done`.
37	  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
38	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
39	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
40	    changed.
41	
42	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
43	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
44	result must always be published at close-out. See
45	[Pushing](#pushing).
46	
47	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
48	warrant its own ladder, it subdivides — `X.Y.Z-3.0`
49	Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
50	Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
51	at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
52	suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
53	for the local-ladder mechanics.
54	
55	## Chores sections
56	
57	A **chores section** is a `##` section in
58	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
59	general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
60	should have a reference to it on a `Commits:` list in a
61	chores file.
62	
63	The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
64	`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
65	with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`),
66	followed by an **empty `Commits:`** line. **Each work commit
67	then appends its own As-built rung + narrative note as it
68	lands** — the chores record is built up per commit, not held
69	back and written all at once at close-out; close-out only
70	*finalizes* (title sync, design subsections, retiring the
71	`## In Progress` block). The `Commits:` line is backfilled
72	later, once the commit is permanent (see
73	[Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
74	
75	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
76	design subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in
77	AGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).
78	
79	### Commits backfill
80	
81	A chores section's `Commits:` line cites the commit(s) it
82	records, by SHA — but a SHA isn't stable until the commit
83	lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
84	release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or
85	squash rewrites it on the way. So:
86	
87	- A chores section is **opened with an empty `Commits:`** line.
88	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
89	  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
90	  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
91	  push later: **each push backfills the `Commits:` of the
92	  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
93	  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands —
94	  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
95	  invalidate.
96	
97	Use `[[N]]` refs — several as `[[N]],[[M]]` only when one
98	section records multiple commits (a merge non-ff close-out) —
99	with the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's `# References`
100	(format in AGENTS.md
101	[Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references)).
102	A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
103	deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
104	`git log --grep "<title>"`.
105	
106	The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma — a
107	**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
108	close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
109	SHA must be permanent.
110	
111	## Preparation
112	
113	The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
114	setup (a lightweight cycle omits it — see
115	[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)):
116	
117	- **Bump the version-of-record** to `X.Y.Z-0`. Where it
118	  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
119	  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
120	  project-specific — see [versioning.md](versioning.md).

# Cycle protocol

This protocol uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.

The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
the conversation — code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
equivalents — this project's manifest is recorded in
[versioning.md](versioning.md).

## Cycles

A cycle has three phases:

- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`) — the cycle's
  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
  it and starts at `-1` — see
  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
  cycle:
  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
    and the suffix scheme are project-specific — see
    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
    statement + plan ladder).
  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) — the
  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
  needs; each runs through the
  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`) — the cycle's
  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
    `## Done`.
  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
    [chores section](#chores-sections).
  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
    changed.

A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
result must always be published at close-out. See
[Pushing](#pushing).

**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
warrant its own ladder, it subdivides — `X.Y.Z-3.0`
Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
for the local-ladder mechanics.

## Chores sections

A **chores section** is a `##` section in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
should have a reference to it on a `Commits:` list in a
chores file.

The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`),
followed by an **empty `Commits:`** line. **Each work commit
then appends its own As-built rung + narrative note as it
lands** — the chores record is built up per commit, not held
back and written all at once at close-out; close-out only
*finalizes* (title sync, design subsections, retiring the
`## In Progress` block). The `Commits:` line is backfilled
later, once the commit is permanent (see
[Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).

Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
design subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in
AGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).

### Commits backfill

A chores section's `Commits:` line cites the commit(s) it
records, by SHA — but a SHA isn't stable until the commit
lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or
squash rewrites it on the way. So:

- A chores section is **opened with an empty `Commits:`** line.
- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
  push later: **each push backfills the `Commits:` of the
  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands —
  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
  invalidate.

Use `[[N]]` refs — several as `[[N]],[[M]]` only when one
section records multiple commits (a merge non-ff close-out) —
with the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's `# References`
(format in AGENTS.md
[Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references)).
A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
`git log --grep "<title>"`.

The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma — a
**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
SHA must be permanent.

The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs

- **Bump the version-of-record** to `X.Y.Z-0`. Where it
  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
  project-specific — see [versioning.md](versioning.md).

184	
185	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes

## Ideas

Longer-range thoughts, not yet ranked work. `-` bullets, no
numbering; promote into `## Todo` when one becomes actionable.

- Per-bench dependency isolation — motivated by dep provenance:
  the deps are the thing being measured, so a dep bump (e.g.
  iceoryx2 0.9.2 → 0.9.3) legitimately moves that bench's
  numbers and shouldn't ride in silently. Options considered
  (2026-07-08):
  - Caveat first: a Cargo **workspace shares one Cargo.lock**
    across members — it scopes deps per package (ice benches
    alone pay for iceoryx2; faster `-p` builds; harness/probes
    become a library crate) but does *not* give per-bench lock
    isolation, and it splits the single CLI into many binaries.
  - Targeted updates (`cargo update -p <crate>`, never bare
    `cargo update`) — ~90% of the provenance benefit at zero
    structure cost; adoptable immediately as discipline.
  - Feature gates (`--features ice`) — solves build weight in
    the current single package, not lock isolation.
  - Truly standalone crates (own Cargo.lock each) — the only
    real per-bench dep isolation; maximum maintenance, and cuts
    against "same harness, same build" A/B comparability.
  - Current lean: targeted-update discipline now; feature gates
    or workspace only when bench families multiply.

  iiac-perf`) would give bash die-hards a compact column view

content.content:
vc-x1 0.71.0

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main` — one resumable command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (tracking / bot-published / sync checks —
no build steps; run project checks yourself before pushing)
→ review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-work → commit-bot (skipped if clean) → bookmark-set
(work repo → <bookmark>, bot repo → main) → push-work →
squash-push-bot. Failures in commit-work / commit-bot /
bookmark-set roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-work.
After push-work succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (flag form; see positional)

  -V, --version
          Print the `vc-x1 X.Y.Z` banner as the first line, then continue. With
          no subcommand, prints the banner and exits.
          
          Replaces clap's auto-version (which would exit after printing): the
          banner now rides along with normal subcommand execution rather than
          gating it, so scripts can capture the version *and* the command's
          output in one invocation.

      --restart
          Clear any saved state file and start from stage 1

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --from <STAGE>
          Explicit stage to jump to (advanced / debug use)

          Possible values:
          - preflight:       Verify bookmark tracking, the bot-published
            invariant, and sync state
          - review:          Present diff for the first approval gate
          - message:         Compose / edit the commit message; present for
            second gate
          - commit-work:     Commit the work repo
          - commit-bot:      Commit the `.claude` bot repo (skipped if empty)
          - bookmark-set:    Advance each repo's bookmark to its `@-`: work →
            `<bookmark>`, bot → `main`
          - push-work:       `jj git push --bookmark <b> -R .`
          - squash-push-bot: In-process squash of `.claude`'s trailing session
            writes + push `main`

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --status
          Print where the saved state thinks we are and exit

      --recheck
          Re-run `preflight` even on resume (default: skip if last run
          succeeded)

      --no-squash-push
          Stop before `squash-push-bot` so it can be run manually

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

      --title <STR>
          Commit title (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

      --body <STR>
          Commit body (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

  -y, --yes
          Auto-approve interactive prompts (review gate, message-edit
          confirmation). Required when `--title` / `--body` aren't both supplied
          in non-interactive contexts

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

content.text:
Short version: a transient failure at the sandbox's network proxy, almost certainly unrelated to your two instances.

The evidence is in the error shape. The failing line was `socat ... W CONNECT github.com:22: Bad Gateway`. In this sandbox, git's SSH traffic is tunneled through socat to an HTTP proxy that enforces the network allowlist; "Bad Gateway" is the proxy saying *it* accepted my request but couldn't establish its upstream leg to github.com:22 at that moment. So the request died between the proxy and GitHub — not in jj, not in the repos, not in anything another session could hold a lock on. Concurrent-instance interference would look different: jj working-copy or op-store lock errors, or a preflight complaint about repo state — all local, all named explicitly. And the definitive test is that the retry succeeded a few minutes later with zero changes on our side.

My guess at the cause (unverifiable from here): either a brief GitHub SSH endpoint blip or the sandbox's proxy process restarting/momentarily unhealthy. Your `cargo clean && cargo build` succeeding in between doesn't discriminate — cargo talks HTTPS to crates.io, a different path than SSH-over-proxy to GitHub — though it does confirm general network health, which points the finger more at the SSH tunnel leg specifically.

The plain version: the phone line between my sandbox and GitHub's SSH door hiccuped for a moment, and the error message names that middleman explicitly. Two sessions sharing the project would fail differently — with complaints about the repo being busy, not about a gateway.

1	//! Generic bench driver: the [`Bench`] trait, adaptive outer/inner
2	//! loop sizing, and the band-histogram report.
3	
4	use std::hint::black_box;
5	
6	use hdrhistogram::Histogram;
7	
8	use crate::bands::{self, BandLabels};
9	use crate::overhead::{Dither, Overhead};
10	
11	const WARMUP: u64 = 10_000;
12	const ESTIMATE_STEPS: u64 = 1_000;
13	const ESTIMATE_SAMPLES: usize = 5;
14	const FRAMING_DOMINATION_RATIO: f64 = 10.0;
15	const MAX_INNER: u64 = 1_000;
16	
17	/// Sleep-separated blocks: random sleep bounds (ms) between
18	/// blocks. Randomized so block boundaries don't phase-lock with
19	/// kernel ticks or workload periodicity; long enough to let the
20	/// scheduler / frequency state re-roll.
21	const BLOCK_SLEEP_MS_MIN: u64 = 1;
22	const BLOCK_SLEEP_MS_MAX: u64 = 10;
23	
24	/// Unrecorded post-wake warm-up per block (seconds) — each wake
25	/// pays a frequency ramp + cache refill (the measured
26	/// cold-calibration effect), which must not leak into the block's
27	/// samples.
28	const BLOCK_WARMUP_SECONDS: f64 = 0.002;
29	
30	/// Histogram value bounds: 1 ps to 60 s at 3 sig figs. Values
31	/// are recorded in **picoseconds** — the timer reads integer ns,
32	/// but dividing a sample by `inner` in ps keeps the true sub-ns
33	/// per-call precision that ns recording truncated (a 4.7 ns call
34	/// no longer rounds to 5). The high bound is a sane-world
35	/// ceiling for one recorded sample, not a technical limit —
36	/// [`record_sample`] clamps above it and [`warn_invalid`] flags
37	/// the run.
38	const HIST_LOW_PS: u64 = 1;
39	const HIST_HIGH_PS: u64 = 60_000_000_000_000;
40	
41	/// Picoseconds per nanosecond: recorded values are ps, display
42	/// is ns.
43	const PS_PER_NS: f64 = 1000.0;
44	
45	/// `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` minus `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` elapsed divergence
46	/// (seconds) at or above which [`warn_invalid`] reports that the
47	/// system suspended during the run.
48	const SUSPEND_WARN_S: f64 = 1.0;
49	
50	/// A benchmark workload: a named operation that `step()` performs
51	/// in a tight loop for sub-µs latency measurement. Implementors own
52	/// any setup state (channels, spawned threads, counters). `step()`
53	/// returns a value so the caller can `black_box` it against dead-code
54	/// elimination.
55	pub trait Bench {
56	    /// Human-readable name used in the report header.
57	    fn name(&self) -> &str;
58	
59	    /// Run one unit of work. Return any value derived from the work
60	    /// to defeat DCE — the caller black-boxes it.
61	    fn step(&mut self) -> u64;
62	}
63	
64	/// Runtime configuration for one [`run_adaptive`] call.
65	#[derive(Debug)]
66	pub struct RunCfg<'a> {
67	    /// Calibrated apparatus overhead (framing + loop/iter) used to
68	    /// compute the `adjusted` mean columns in the report.
69	    pub overhead: &'a Overhead,
70	    /// Wall-clock seconds budget for time-based runs. Ignored when
71	    /// `outer_override` is set.
72	    pub target_seconds: f64,
73	    /// Force a fixed outer-loop count, bypassing the time budget.
74	    pub outer_override: Option<u64>,
75	    /// Force a fixed inner-loop count, bypassing the
76	    /// overhead-dominated auto-sizing.
77	    pub inner_override: Option<u64>,
78	    /// Core pool for thread pinning. Indexed positionally with
79	    /// wrap-around via [`core_for`][RunCfg::core_for]; empty means
80	    /// no pinning.
81	    pub pin_cores: &'a [usize],
82	    /// When set, [`crate::tprobe::TProbe::report`] emits raw TSC
83	    /// ticks instead of nanoseconds. Plumbed from the `-t/--ticks`
84	    /// CLI flag.
85	    pub report_ticks: bool,
86	    /// Band-label style for [`print_report`] histogram rows.
87	    /// Plumbed from the `--band-labels` CLI flag.
88	    pub band_labels: BandLabels,
89	    /// Decimal digits on [`print_report`] time columns. Plumbed
90	    /// from the `--decimals` CLI flag (default 1; 0 restores
91	    /// integers; 3 is the ps recording floor).
92	    pub decimals: usize,
93	    /// Split the run into this many sleep-separated blocks and
94	    /// report block-replication stats (mean ± 95% CI, LSC).
95	    /// Plumbed from the `--blocks` CLI flag; `None` = single
96	    /// continuous run. See
97	    /// notes/design.md#within-invocation-replication-sleep-separated-blocks.
98	    pub blocks: Option<u64>,
99	}
100	
101	impl RunCfg<'_> {
102	    /// CPU id for the bench's `thread_idx`-th thread, using
103	    /// wrap-around over the pool. Returns `None` when the pool is
104	    /// empty so callers can treat unpinned and pinned runs uniformly.
105	    pub fn core_for(&self, thread_idx: usize) -> Option<usize> {
106	        if self.pin_cores.is_empty() {
107	            None
108	        } else {
109	            Some(self.pin_cores[thread_idx % self.pin_cores.len()])
110	        }
111	    }
112	}
113	
114	/// Block-replication statistics from a sleep-separated run —
115	/// each block is a mini-run (own sleep re-roll + warm-up), so the
116	/// spread of block means yields an honest-per-invocation CI and
117	/// LSC. See
118	/// notes/design.md#within-invocation-replication-sleep-separated-blocks.
119	#[derive(Debug)]
120	pub struct BlockStats {
121	    /// Number of blocks (Y).
122	    pub blocks: u64,
123	    /// Mean of the per-block means, ns.
124	    pub mean_ns: f64,
125	    /// 95% confidence half-width on `mean_ns`:

130	    pub lsc_ns: f64,
131	}

message.content: Advantages/disadvantages of the more inners/less?

content.text:
This trade sits at the heart of the harness design, so worth laying out both directions carefully.

**Larger `inner` (more calls per sample):**

- *Amortization* — the per-sample framing (~25 ns of timer apparatus) spreads over more calls: at `inner=24` the residue is ~1 ns/call, at `inner=9` ~2.8 ns, at `inner=1` the full 25 ns rides on every reading. This is the reason `pick_inner` exists.
- *Resolution* — dividing elapsed by `inner` yields sub-quantum per-call precision (the ps-recording point): a 22.3 ns call is distinguishable from 22.5 ns only when the timer quantum is spread over many calls.
- *Less apparatus perturbation* — fewer timer reads per unit time; more of the run's wall clock is actual workload.

**Smaller `inner` (fewer calls per sample):**

- *Distribution fidelity* — this is the big one. Each sample is the **mean** of its `inner` calls, so the histogram is a distribution of small means, not of calls. A 200 ns hiccup inside a 1000-call sample surfaces as +0.2 ns/call — invisible; inside a 10-call sample it's +20 ns — a visible tail event. Large `inner` smears exactly the tail and mode structure TProbe exists to expose, and it dilutes the interference-crossover analysis (band counts stop counting *events*).
- *Interference localization* — a preemption contaminates one short sample rather than poisoning a long one covering thousands of calls; the census can then count and discard it. Longer samples are also individually more likely to catch a hit (probability scales with sample duration).
- *Statistics and time axis* — more samples per second means finer percentile resolution and, relevant to the batch pipeline, a finer-grained time axis for drift and burst localization.

So neither direction is free: **large `inner` trades distribution truth for low apparatus bias; small `inner` trades bias for truth.** That's why the sizing rule is "just enough and no more" — `inner ≈ 10 × frame/step` pushes the framing residue down to ~10% of a step and then stops, preserving as much tail fidelity as the bias budget allows, with `MAX_INNER` capping the smear for very fast steps. It's also why yesterday's change deserves its flag: halving `inner` (9 vs ~24) *gains* tail fidelity and localization but *spends* bias budget (~11% residue vs ~5%). One more subtlety for A/B use: the framing residue only fully cancels between runs whose `inner` matches; two benches auto-sized to different `inner` carry different residues, which is inherent to auto-sizing and unchanged from before.

The plain version: each recorded number is really the average of a little burst of calls. Long bursts hide the measurement tool's cost nicely, but they also blur out the very spikes and hiccups we're trying to see — a spike averaged over a thousand calls vanishes. Short bursts show every spike clearly but let the tool's cost bleed into the numbers. So we make the bursts just long enough to keep the tool's cost small, and no longer.

content.text:
This pair of runs is a textbook illustration of the trade we just discussed — including one genuinely satisfying confirmation hiding in the tails.

**The tail dilution math checks out exactly.** Multiply the n5 band value by `inner` in each run: 146.7 ns × 15 ≈ 2.20 µs, and 291.6 ns × 7 ≈ 2.04 µs. Same underlying ~2.1 µs interference event on both runs — the number in the table is just that event divided by how many calls shared its sample. The `inner=7` run reports tail spikes at nearly twice the per-call magnitude because they're diluted half as much, and it caught more of them per sample count (n5: 2,450 of 28.6M vs 1,858 of 16.8M). That's the fidelity gain, live.

**The mean shift is only partly explained by the known bias.** The framing arithmetic predicts: `frame/sample`/`inner` goes from 7.0/15 ≈ 0.47 ns to 7.0/7 ≈ 1.0 ns — about +0.5 ns of extra apparatus residue per call (the printed `adj/call` 0.83 → 1.36 says the same). But the raw mean moved +1.3 ns (16.5 → 17.8), and the whole mode structure shifted (dominant mode 16.7 → 17.2/18.6, the 16.0 floor band gone entirely). The extra ~0.8 ns isn't the residue — the calibration blocks are near-identical (frame/call 22.812 vs 22.803, both grade A), so the machine state matches. We think it's the codegen sensitivity the 0.22 cycle kept measuring: two different binaries, and the sample loop's surrounding code moved — the exact class of ~1 ns effect Replanning II decided to stop chasing and let common-mode cancellation absorb. Which it does — *within* one binary. Comparing across versions, as you just did, is precisely where it shows.

**The decision this data sharpens:** with -2 about to make raw the only reported number, `inner` choices move the headline directly. Options:

- **Keep ratio 10** (current): ~1 ns visible residue on ~17 ns steps, better tail fidelity and localization — which is what the -4 gauge and crossover analysis feed on.
- **Bump `FRAMING_DOMINATION_RATIO` to 20**: `inner` returns to ~14–15, residue back to ~0.5 ns, raw means comparable with your historical tables — at the cost of re-diluting tail events ~2× and halving sample count.

My lean is ratio 20: the tail-fidelity loss is modest (events at 145 ns are still far above the 18 ns bulk — the crossover analysis survives dilution fine), while a headline number that's ~6% apparatus is the kind of thing raw-only reporting shouldn't carry when 0.5 ns is available for free. Your call — one constant either way.

The plain version: the two runs agree beautifully once you know each reported number is an average over a burst — the same 2-microsecond hiccup shows up twice as tall in the new run because it's shared among half as many calls. The new run's average is about 1.3 ns higher: roughly 0.5 ns is the measuring tool showing through more (expected, fixable with one constant), and the rest is the compiler laying out the two binaries slightly differently — the noise floor we've decided to live with. I'd nudge the constant so the tool shows through less, since soon the raw number is the only one printed.

message.content: Personally, tail events are not useful for performance tuning, is that claim true?

content.text:
Mostly true for what *this project* measures, with one carve-out worth keeping sharp — and your own crossover analysis (the interference-crossover Todo) already contains the precise version of the claim.

The case where you're right: for ns-scale operations on a general-purpose OS, the far tail is the *machine*, not the code. The counting argument from the min-now analysis says it directly — n4+ events arrive at ~1,500/s, timer-interrupt territory; nothing in a 17 ns code path produces a 2 µs excursion. Preemptions, IRQs, SMIs land on whatever instruction is executing regardless of whose it is. So for performance *tuning* — choosing implementation A over B — those events carry zero information about the code: both candidates would eat the same interrupts. Tuning against them is chasing the room again. That's exactly why the trimmed-core-stats Todo exists (the full mean wobbles ±1.4% with the mode mix while the p10–p90 core holds ±0.2%): the comparable number is the bulk, tails excluded.

The carve-out: not everything off the main mode is machine. Code has *legitimate* occasional slow paths — an allocation, a rehash, a ring wrap, a lock briefly contended, a channel's blocking fallback — and those are real, tunable properties that distinguish implementations. The crossover is the dividing line: below it (your n2/n3 at rates no OS mechanism can produce), rare-but-fast events are code and useful; above it, events at OS-mechanism rates are machine and useless for tuning. For IIAC comparisons specifically — where "spin vs blocking wait" is a design axis — that below-crossover structure is signal you'd want. (The one context where far tails are genuinely the tuning target is p99-SLO / real-time work, but measuring *code* tails there requires an isolated machine — on a desktop the machine's tail swamps the code's.)

Two consequences for the work in flight. First, tails keep their *other* job: they grade the run — interference rate, burst localization, "was this run quiet enough to trust" — which is diagnostic value, not tuning value, and it's the whole -4 design. Second, this settles the ratio question more firmly in favor of 20: my "tail fidelity" argument for small `inner` was mostly about resolving above-crossover events more sharply, and if those are non-actionable for tuning — needed only at "countable and attributable" fidelity, which survives 2× dilution fine — then trading them for a cleaner headline mean is the right side of the bargain.

The plain version: yes — for deciding which code is faster, the rare huge spikes are almost always the operating system interrupting, not your code, and both versions of your code suffer them equally, so they can't help you choose. The exception is moderately-rare slowness the code itself causes (a queue occasionally doing extra work) — that does distinguish implementations and lives closer to the bulk of the data. The spikes still earn their keep for a different job: telling you whether the machine was quiet enough for the run to be trusted.

message.content: One other kinda-of-related what if only 1%, 20% or 50% of the measurement time was spent measuring the other were quiet time so that we maybe reduce the number of times the OS interrupts us and we reduce the noise?

content.text:
Good instinct to question, but the naive version of the hope — "measure less of the time, get interrupted less *per measured second*" — mostly doesn't hold, and one of its side effects is actively poisonous on your hardware. There are two real second-order effects in its favor, though, so it's worth taking apart. Also: the harness can already run this experiment.

**Why the core hope fails:** the dominant interference (timer ticks, IRQs) arrives at a roughly constant *rate while you're running*. Quiet time doesn't bank credit — the moment you resume measuring, ticks hit your measuring windows at the same rate as before. Contaminated-sample fraction ≈ event rate × sample duration, and neither factor changes with duty cycle. At a 1% duty cycle you wait 100× longer for the same statistics and the same ~1,500/s events land in your measured seconds all the same.

**The two effects that are real:**

- *Scheduler kindness.* Some preemptions are punishment for hogging: exhaust your quantum and CFS/EEVDF evicts you. A task that sleeps regularly rarely exhausts its quantum and accumulates scheduling goodwill, so the involuntary-preemption class (the big, rare events) genuinely thins. This is a real mechanism, though on an otherwise-idle box with free cores it's a small population to begin with.
- *Thermal headroom.* Continuous spin heats the die; on boost-limited parts clocks sag over a long run (drift). A 50% duty cycle keeps the silicon cooler and boost sustained — potentially *less* drift on thermally-limited machines.

**The effect that kills it here:** quiet time is exactly what invites the frequency governor to downclock — and then every measuring window starts with a ramp. That's the 7600x-F mechanism from Replanning II, deliberately self-inflicted at every wake. Plus each wake pays cache refill and warmup tax (the existing `--blocks` mode budgets 2 ms of unrecorded warmup per wake for precisely this reason). So duty cycling trades a modest reduction in one noise class (preemption) for systematic exposure to the noise class that's actually been hurting us (frequency regimes), while dividing sample throughput by the duty factor.

**The good news — this is testable today, not arguable.** `--blocks` *is* duty-cycled measurement: random 1–10 ms sleeps between blocks, post-wake warmup, per-block stats. Run `min-now` continuous vs `--blocks` at a few block counts (which sweeps the effective duty fraction), same total measure time, and compare the n4+ event rate and the disturbed %. If the sleep-separated runs show a meaningfully lower interference rate, your idea earns a knob; my prediction is the rate stays flat while block means wobble more from ramp effects. And once the -4 gauge lands, it quantifies exactly this per run (interference rate from census counts, drift from batch floors) — so the question graduates from prediction to routine measurement. Worth a line in `## Ideas` if you want it kept: "duty-cycle experiment — does sleep-separated measuring reduce interference rate? testable via --blocks."

The plain version: the interruptions come at a steady drumbeat whenever you're running — resting between measurements doesn't make the drum quieter during them, it just means you measure less. Resting does earn you two small favors (the scheduler picks on busy tasks more than polite ones, and a cooler chip keeps its speed up), but it also invites the CPU to nap along with you, and waking it up slow is the very problem we've been fighting. Luckily the tool already has a rest-between-blocks mode, so we can measure whether your idea helps on your machines instead of debating it.

message.content:
Here's a crazy idea we determine the timer interrupts and we move our measurements between
them as they happen regularly and we maybe sleep some to be nice but measure hard so the
clocks don't slow down, actually with cpupower set at performance that should be less of a problem?

content.text:
Not crazy at all — you've reinvented a real technique (tick-phase avoidance), and it's cheap enough to be feasible. But before endorsing it, worth being precise about what it buys and what already-simpler moves buy first.

**Why it's feasible:** the scheduler tick is periodic per-CPU (Arch kernels run CONFIG_HZ=300, so every ~3.3 ms) and each hit costs a few µs — which is exactly what makes it both predictable and dodgeable. Detect a tick hit (it's a huge, unmistakable outlier in a ~17 ns sample stream), note its timestamp, predict the next at +3.3 ms, and pause measuring for a ~20–50 µs window around the prediction. The arithmetic is friendly: you sacrifice ~1% of wall time, so this is *not* the duty-cycling case from your last question — the machine stays ~99% busy, the governor never sees idle, and yes, with `cpupower -g performance` (plus EPP `performance` on the amd-pstate boxes — the Replanning II machine-side fix) the ramp concern is essentially retired. The "sleep some to be nice" part you can skip entirely: on an idle multicore box, one spinning core inconveniences nobody.

**Why the payoff is smaller than it looks:** we already *detect* every tick hit after the fact — they're the n4+ bands — and the trimmed bulk stats already exclude them, so dodging ticks doesn't improve the headline numbers at all. What it genuinely buys is a **cleaner tail**: with the periodic ~300/s contaminant surgically removed, whatever remains above the crossover is the rare, aperiodic stuff (device IRQs, SMIs, real code slow paths) — currently drowned out at ~10× lower rates. That directly serves the crossover analysis and the gauge, not tuning. One design tension to note: the dither machinery exists to prevent accidental *phase-locking* with ticks; deliberate *anti-phase* scheduling is its aggressive cousin and would need care not to introduce a systematic phase bias in what's measured (probably negligible, but it's the kind of thing this project has learned to check rather than assume).

**The cheaper ladder to climb first:** (1) governor+EPP performance — config, zero code, fixes ramps; (2) pin the bench away from core 0, which the placement map showed eats the IRQ load; (3) IRQ affinity, moving device interrupts off the bench core — root config, no code; (4) the endgame for lab-grade runs is `nohz_full`/`isolcpus` boot parameters, which don't dodge the tick but *abolish* it on the isolated core (down to 1 Hz) — strictly stronger than any in-harness cleverness, at the cost of a reboot and dedicated cores. Tick-dodging's niche is "cleaner tails on an unmodified machine," which is respectable — it keeps the tool useful on boxes you can't reconfigure.

Worth an `## Ideas` entry? Something like: "tick-phase avoidance — predict per-CPU scheduler ticks from detected hits, pause measurement ~30 µs around each; ~1% duty cost, no governor exposure at performance/EPP-performance; buys cleaner above-crossover tails on unmodified machines; compare against nohz_full isolation before building." Say the word and I'll add it.

The plain version: the operating system's metronome ticks about 300 times a second on the busy core, and each tick briefly stomps on whatever's running. Since the ticks are regular, we really could learn their rhythm and step aside just before each one — it costs about 1% of our time and, with the CPU speed pinned high like you said, no slowdown risk. The catch: we already spot and discard the stomped measurements, so the average doesn't improve — what improves is our view of the *rare* disturbances currently hidden behind the regular ones. And there's a boot setting that silences the metronome on a chosen core entirely, which beats dodging it — when you're allowed to reboot the machine.

Great catch — but no, it's not the keystroke. The keystroke theory predicts the wrong signature: handling a keypress costs the OS a few µs of interrupt and terminal work, which would land as a handful of *disturbed samples* — and the disturbed counts are essentially identical across all four runs (0.45–0.52% d_high, 0.01–0.02% d_low). What actually differs is the *speed the whole machine ran at*, and that points at frequency state, not I/O.

Look at `loop/iter`: the quick-repeat runs measure 0.438 ns/iter, the waited runs 0.489 — the same loop running **11.6% faster** in the quick-repeat case. That's a clock-frequency ratio, not noise (and `ticks/ns` is identical to 6 digits in all runs — the TSC doesn't care, only the core clock moved).
