content.text:
Because the grade doesn't score *speed* — it scores *agreement with itself*. Every signal in it (drift bracket, repeat, attempt-vs-attempt) measures whether the machine held one state through the ~600 ms window. A steadily slow machine aces that test; a fast machine caught changing gears flunks it. The letter answers "can these numbers be trusted to describe one consistent machine?", not "was the machine quick?"

And your quick repeats weren't "already up to speed" — that's the subtle part. Look at what the signals actually caught:

- First quick run: drift bracket 48.574 → 45.348. It *started* at 48.6 — neither the settled 50.4 nor the fast 45.3, but partway between — and was still accelerating through the calibration. If the core had truly held the previous run's speed, `l_start` would already be 45.3 and drift would be ~0%.
- Second quick run: drift only 0.62%, but the two calibration attempts inside the run disagreed by 22.5% (repeat ±4.96 ns) — the state was still wobbling between attempts.

So the fast state is **transient, not held**: the moment a run ends, boost management starts relaxing the core toward its equilibrium, and your ~2 s of uparrow-and-return is enough for it to slide partway back. Each quick relaunch therefore catches the core mid-slide and re-accelerating — measuring *during the gear change*. The waited runs catch it after the slide completes, at the equilibrium — slower, but the same speed at the start, middle, and end of the window, and the same speed on both attempts. Consistency is what a calibration constant needs, because it's about to be arithmetically combined with (and in the old design, subtracted from) measurements taken moments later: a constant measured at 46-and-changing describes no state the bench will actually run in, while one measured at a flat 50.4 describes at least one real state exactly.

Your intuition would be right in a different protocol, though: if the load were *continuous* — calibration starting within milliseconds of sustained prior load, no gap — the fast state might hold through the window and grade well *and* fast. That's essentially what the warm-until-stable design (Todo #1) buys: keep loading until consecutive passes agree, so you enter measurement inside whatever state is currently steady, high or low, instead of at a moment your shell history timing happens to pick.

The plain version: the score isn't "how fast was the machine" but "did it stay the same the whole time we measured." Re-running quickly doesn't catch the machine warmed-up-and-steady — it catches it half-relaxed from the last run and speeding back up, so the beginning and end of the measurement disagree, and the tool rightly says "don't trust this pair of numbers together." Waiting catches it parked at its steady speed: slower, but the same slower everywhere, which is the thing a measurement can actually use.

- **The idle→load frequency ramp is fast** — on a CPPC/schedutil AMD box under a hard spin, the transition from idle clocks to load clocks completes in roughly milliseconds to tens of milliseconds. Calibration doesn't start its graded measurement at t=0: there's warmup and the `w_low`/`l_low` phase before the loop-only ladder whose endpoints form the drift bracket. By the time `l_start` is measured, the from-idle ramp finished long ago. It's invisible not because it didn't happen but because it happened *before the graded window opened*. Hence 50.357 → 50.357, drift 0.00%.
- **The boost-state relaxation is slow** — the decay from the fast ~45.3 state back toward the ~50.4 equilibrium (and the re-entry when load resumes) plays out over hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. We think it's boost/thermal-budget governance rather than simple P-state switching. That timescale is *comparable to the calibration window*, which is exactly the condition for the bracket to catch it mid-flight: your first quick run opened at 48.6 (partway down the slide) and closed at 45.3 — 6.6% inside the window.

So the grade isn't "ramps degrade it"; it's "state changes *that straddle the measurement window* degrade it." A transition much faster than the window completes before the bracket opens and shows nothing. One much slower than the window moves too little in 600 ms to trip a threshold. The quick-repeat case is the unlucky middle: your uparrow cadence (~2 s) matches the boost-relaxation timescale, parking every run right on top of the transition.

And to connect it to the earlier 7600x story, since they look contradictory: there, the from-idle ramp *did* poison calibration — but that box was deep-idling with a conservative governor, making its idle→load ramp a *slow* (governor-timescale, tens-to-hundreds of ms) process that the ~40 µs `CAL_WARMUP` couldn't outlast. Same principle, different machine: the grade sees whatever process happens to be rate-matched to its window, and which process that is depends on each box's governor and boost behavior. That window-relativity is also the quiet argument for both of the queued designs: warm-until-stable enters measurement only after transitions stop (whatever their timescale), and the batch pipeline stretches the observation window across the whole run, so slow processes that a 600 ms bracket can't resolve become visible as batch-floor trends.

The plain version: the grade only notices a speed change if it happens *while* the grade is watching. Starting from a standstill, the CPU reaches its steady speed in a few milliseconds — over before the watching starts, so the waited runs look perfectly stable. The after-run cool-down you interrupt with a quick re-run takes a couple of seconds — the same length as the watch window — so those runs get caught mid-change every time. #!/usr/bin/env bash
# Reproduce the quick-repeat settle anomaly (3900X, 2026-07-27):
# calibrate runs launched ~2 s apart catch the core mid-relaxation
# between its fast transient and slow equilibrium and grade D/F,
# while runs spaced ~8 s apart measure the settled state and grade
# B. The dynamic-warmup fix (TODO.md Todo "Dynamic startup
# warmup") is accepted when both cadences agree.
#
# - usage: scripts/settle-anomaly.sh [binary]
#   binary defaults to `iiac-perf` on PATH; pass a saved failing
#   build (e.g. ./iiac-perf-0.23.0-1) once `calibrate` is gone
#   from the repo.
# - env knobs: N (runs per cadence, default 5), QUICK_GAP (s,
#   default 2), WAIT_GAP (s, default 8).
# - run on a quiet box: a live bot session or desktop load
#   depresses grades in both cadences and masks the contrast.
# - judgment is majority-of-N by eye: anomaly present = quick
#   rows mostly D/F while waited rows mostly A/B; fixed = the
#   two cadences produce the same letters and stable loop/iter.
set -euo pipefail

bin="${1:-iiac-perf}"
n="${N:-5}"
quick_gap="${QUICK_GAP:-2}"
wait_gap="${WAIT_GAP:-8}"

run_one() {
    local out
    out="$("$bin" calibrate 2>&1)"
    local letter drift repeat loop_iter
    letter="$(awk '/^  environment/{print $2}' <<<"$out")"
    drift="$(grep -o 'drift [0-9.]*%' <<<"$out" | head -1)"
    repeat="$(grep -o 'repeat ±[0-9.]* ns' <<<"$out" | head -1)"
    loop_iter="$(awk '/^  loop\/iter/{print $2}' <<<"$out")"
    printf '%-8s %-3s loop/iter %-8s %-14s %s\n' \
        "$1" "$letter" "$loop_iter" "$drift" "$repeat"
}

echo "settle-anomaly: $("$bin" -V 2>/dev/null | head -1 || echo "$bin")"
echo "N=$n quick_gap=${quick_gap}s wait_gap=${wait_gap}s"
echo

echo "quick cadence (gap ${quick_gap}s — expect D/F while unfixed):"
for i in $(seq "$n"); do
    sleep "$quick_gap"
    run_one "quick-$i"
done
echo

echo "waited cadence (gap ${wait_gap}s — expect A/B):"
for i in $(seq "$n"); do
    sleep "$wait_gap"
    run_one "wait-$i"
done

The distinction isn't sleep vs. no sleep; it's **experiment vs. assertion**. - **The cadence** — yes, `sleep` controls this perfectly. That part automates fine.
- **The hardware's personality** — the anomaly exists because *this* 3900X, under *this* governor config, has a ~2 s two-state boost relaxation. The 7600x may not show it at all; a CI runner or VM certainly won't (pinned clocks, or noisy-neighbor chaos). A test asserting "quick cadence grades worse" fails on healthy code wherever the hardware lacks the behavior — and after the fix, a pass can't distinguish "code fixed" from "this machine never showed it anyway."
- **Ambient quiet** — and the smoke test just demonstrated this beautifully: it came back *inverted* (quick-1 got C, wait-1 got F with repeat ±6.91) because I ran it with zero gaps *while a bot session was live on the box* — the exact contaminated-run scenario from the 0.22 close-out validation. Any automated assertion inherits that flakiness in both directions.

So the reproducer is real and scripted, but the *judgment* stays with a human running it deliberately: right machine, quiet conditions, majority-of-N, eyes on the letter pattern. That's also why it's a bash script around the binary rather than a `#[test]`: a cargo test can only exercise the code currently in the tree, but this test's whole design needs to run the **saved failing binary** (0.23.0-1, whose `calibrate` still exists) side by side with future fixed builds — an external artifact cargo tests can't reach.

If you want a middle ground later, the script's judgment could be automated *for your known-good conditions* — "on the 3900X, quiet, exit nonzero if the cadences disagree by more than a letter" — as a close-out checklist item rather than CI. But the human-run form is the honest one until the gauge lands and gives it a better observable than the doomed calibrate grade.

The bug lives in how this particular CPU shifts gears, so the test only means something on a machine that has those gears and nothing else going on. A build server has different gears or none, so an automated pass/fail there would lie in both directions. Hence: a script anyone can run on the right machine and judge by eye, not a test the robot runs anywhere.

That's actually superior to calling `main` in-process here — each run gets a fresh process exactly like your terminal runs, and two in-process `main` calls would share warmed-up state and not reproduce the cadence effect at all. # Chores 05

Continuation of [chores-04](chores-04.md). Records landed work;
conventions in [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions) and
[cycle-protocol.md](../cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

## feat: grade the run from raw batches

Commits: [[1]]

Decided in
[Replanning II](chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run):
the overhead subtraction estimates an ill-defined quantity —
additivity is an approximation on a superscalar CPU, the
constants moved ~10% with frequency regimes, and the correction
cancels in same-harness A/B anyway — while the calibration-time
grade certified a ~1 s window *before* the run: the room, not
the exam. This cycle removes the adjustment machinery and moves
grading onto the run's own time-ordered batch data.

  micro-probe (low quantile over back-to-back timer pairs)
  instead of `cfg.overhead.frame_call_ns`; sizing no longer
  depends on startup calibration

content.text:
Done — the Rust test replaces the bash script (deleted), and everything is green: clippy clean, default `cargo test` shows it properly ignored (36 unit tests unaffected), and the print-only smoke run parses both cadences.

To answer the original question crisply: `main()` itself is uncallable from an integration test (it lives in the binary crate, which tests can't link), but Cargo's `CARGO_BIN_EXE_iiac-perf` gives every integration test the path to the compiled binary, and spawning it per run is the more faithful reproduction anyway — fresh process, fresh state, exactly like your uparrow-return.

The **-1 commit's scope grows by one deliverable** (this was worth doing mid-rung to capture the baseline before `calibrate` dies at -2): `tests/settle_anomaly.rs` rides with the micro-probe work, and the chores rung + Todo #1 bullet now record it. Still at the ready-to-commit gate — the amended -1 working copy holds the harness change, the test, the version bump, the ref backfills, and today's Ideas/Todo additions.

One suggestion for when it lands: run the real thing once on the 3900X with no bot session and paste the output — `cargo test --release --test settle_anomaly -- --ignored --nocapture` — and we'll have the recorded failing baseline (expect the assertion to *fail* with quick ≈ D/F vs waited ≈ B). That output belongs in the dynamic-warmup chores section when that cycle opens.

content.text:
Yes in principle, but not aimed at `calibrate` — that output has two commits to live. The way I'd cut it:

- **Now:** leave the test's parsing as-is. It's two `strip_prefix` matches on lines this cycle already plans to delete, and if the format drifts the `expect`s fail loudly with a clear message — brittle-but-honest is fine for a two-line parse with a short lifespan.
- **The durable version:** a machine-readable report mode (`--format json`, or key=value lines if we'd rather not take on `serde_json`) designed *when the batch gauge lands* (-4), covering the surface that will actually persist — report stats, gauge signals, letter grade. At that point it serves not just this test but everything that keeps wanting to scrape the report: the placement-map validation runs, cross-run comparison scripts, your terminal experiments. It also dovetails with the unit-scaling Todo, which already wants `--units ns` for "script-stable output" — same underlying need, one flag family.

The general principle I'd apply: a machine-readable flag earns its keep when the *consumers* are stable, and right now the report itself is mid-redesign. Adding it to today's output would mean specifying a schema for numbers scheduled to disappear, then re-specifying at -4.

Adding it to the Todo list next to its sibling concern:

content.text:
The reproduction is locked in. Summary of where the test design landed after this session of iterating against real hardware:

- **Trigger**: zero-gap quick cadence (defaults changed) — a 2 s gap is only ~18% duty and never wakes the boost climb; back-to-back runs reliably shift the core into the fast state mid-window.
- **Criterion**: both cadence medians ≥ B. Not "cadences agree" — a bistable machine honestly measured may report two speeds; what the fix must deliver is that every run measures a *steady* state, so grades (not values) are the assertion.
- **Status**: fails today (medians 3/3), and the run just recorded is the failing baseline. One caveat noted in the Todo entry: this baseline was taken with my session live on the box, which may depress grades somewhat — a quiet-box run from your terminal (`cargo test --release --test settle_anomaly -- --ignored --nocapture`) would make a cleaner "before" record, but the reproduction no longer depends on it.

All of it — test, corrected Todo #1 mechanism note (bistable, transitions straddling windows in both directions), micro-probe work — still sits at the -1 ready-to-commit gate.

The plain version: the test now provokes the misbehavior on demand — hammer the machine with back-to-back runs and it shifts gears mid-measurement, and the test correctly cries foul. It will only go quiet when the warmup fix teaches each run to wait for the gear change to finish before measuring. We caught it on tape while it's still broken, which is what makes it a real before/after test.

message.content: How can I test it

content.text:
From your terminal in the repo root (best with this bot session idle — just don't send me anything while it runs, ~1 minute):

```
cargo test --release --test settle_anomaly -- --ignored --nocapture
```

What you should see while unfixed: a table of ten runs — quick cadence back-to-back (expect the first run or two at `loop/iter 0.489`, then the climb into ~0.445 with D/F/C grades), then the waited cadence at 8 s gaps — followed by the assertion **failing** with `settle anomaly: cadence medians quick N / waited N below B`. That failure is the anomaly reproducing; after the dynamic-warmup fix lands, the same command should pass.

Knobs if you want to poke at it:

- `SETTLE_N=10` — more runs per cadence (default 5).
- `SETTLE_QUICK_GAP=2` — you'll see the anomaly *disappear* (18% duty never triggers the climb; both cadences sit at 0.489 and pass). A nice control experiment.
- `SETTLE_WAIT_GAP=20` — test whether a longer settle actually gets the waited cadence back to B on your box (8 s wasn't always enough after the hammering).
- `SETTLE_PRINT_ONLY=1` — table only, no assertion.
- `IIAC_PERF_BIN=~/iiac-perf-0.23.0-1` — point it at your saved binary instead of the freshly built one (this is how the test stays useful after `calibrate` is deleted at -2).

Two notes on interpreting: the `--release` matters (a debug-build binary has different timing, and `CARGO_BIN_EXE` points at the profile you build with); and grades on a box with a desktop session, browser, etc. can come out depressed in both cadences — the signature to trust is the `loop/iter` column flipping between ~0.489 and ~0.445 alongside bad letters in the quick rows.

message.content: I'm curious why use environment variables instead of parameters?

content.text:
Because in a `cargo test` run, the command line isn't ours to use. The arguments after `--` go to libtest — the test harness Rust compiles into every `#[test]` binary — and it accepts only its own vocabulary (`--ignored`, `--nocapture`, name filters, …). An unrecognized `--settle-n 10` makes it error out, and there's no pass-through mechanism for custom flags. Environment variables are the standard escape hatch: they ride through `cargo` → test binary → `std::env::var` untouched, no parser involved.

There are two ways to get real parameters, each with a cost that didn't seem worth it here:

- **`harness = false`** in Cargo.toml for this test target — you write your own `main()` and own the CLI completely. But you lose everything libtest provides: `#[test]`/`#[ignore]` semantics, `--ignored` gating, name filtering, the pass/FAIL reporting that makes it feel like a test. For one test with four knobs, that's trading the whole point (it's a *test*, run via the test workflow) for nicer argument syntax.
- **Move the knobs into `iiac-perf` itself** — a real subcommand with real clap flags. But that puts acceptance-test orchestration into the product binary, which is the wrong direction; the product's job ends at producing the grade.

There's also a small ergonomic upside to env vars for this particular test: `SETTLE_QUICK_GAP=2 cargo test ...` reads as "same test, different condition," which is exactly the control-experiment usage — the variable applies to the invocation without editing anything.

The plain version: the test-runner program owns the command line and rejects options it doesn't recognize, so tests can't have their own flags. Environment variables are the side door everyone uses; the alternatives — replacing the test-runner or teaching the main program to test itself — cost more than they're worth for a few tuning knobs.

content.text:
That's a fair push, and it moves me — the line I drew ("the product's job ends at the grade") is cleaner than the product's actual philosophy. The grading system exists precisely because this tool treats "can you trust this measurement?" as part of the measurement. And there's strong precedent inside the product already: the calibration self-checks *repeat* the measurement and compare attempts ("constants differ 22.5% between attempts"), and `--blocks` deliberately sleeps and re-measures to expose cross-window instability. Both are the product validating its environment by orchestrating repetition. A cadence-stability check is the same species, one ring further out.

So let me restate the boundary more honestly:

- **In the product's scope** (by its own established philosophy): "measure repeatedly under varied launch/timing conditions and report whether the environment holds still" — a `selftest`- or `--repeat N --gap S`-style mode. It could even own the fresh-process part: a subcommand can respawn its own binary via `current_exe()`, which is exactly what the reproduction needs. And it would answer a question users legitimately ask this tool: "is my box currently trustworthy for A/B?"
- **In the test's scope**: only the thin assertion — invoke that mode, check the verdict, fail loudly. At which point the env-var awkwardness dissolves too: the knobs become real clap flags on the product subcommand, and the integration test barely needs configuration at all. Your instinct about parameters was pulling toward the right architecture.

Why I'd still not build it this week: the product surface it belongs to is mid-demolition. The gauge (-4) is about to become the product's voice for "was this run trustworthy," and a cadence-stability mode should be built *on* the gauge (run N times, compare gauge grades and batch floors) rather than on the calibrate letter that dies at -2. Building it now means building it twice. The env-var test is the disposable scaffold that holds the reproduction while that surface is rebuilt — and its knobs' ugliness is proportionate to its life expectancy.

Worth capturing so the endpoint doesn't get lost: an Ideas entry along the lines of "stability selftest mode — product subcommand that respawns itself N times at configurable cadence and reports cross-run gauge agreement; subsumes `tests/settle_anomaly.rs`'s orchestration (test reduces to asserting on its verdict, env-var knobs become clap flags); build on the batch gauge, not before it." Want me to add it?

The plain version: you're right that this tool's identity includes checking whether the room is steady, not just taking the reading — it already re-measures and compares in two places, and "does my launch timing change the answer" is a natural third. I'd still park the test's crude version where it is for now, because the part of the product this feature should plug into is being rebuilt this cycle — build the plug after the socket exists, and then the test shrinks to almost nothing.

Your data actually reveals the full shape of the thing — and it sharpens one point: it's not that *waiting* is better, it's that **steadiness** is better, and the 0,0 case is steady from the other side. Three regimes are now visible across all our experiments:

- **Continuous hammering** (your 0,0 runs): the box locks into the fast state (0.445) and *stays* — and grades B, honestly, because each window sees one steady machine. Note quick-1 at 0.489 and quick-2 F in three of your four invocations: that F is the single transition run, caught mid-climb, and after it the stream is steady.
- **Fully settled** (long gaps, cold approach): steady at 0.489 — also B.
- **Intermediate cadence** — the danger zone: gaps long enough to start settling, short enough that the next run interrupts it, so *every* window straddles a transition. That's your original ~1 s uparrow cadence, and it's why my quick-0/wait-8 run failed on the *waited* leg — 8 s on a previously-hot box is the danger cadence.

So the anomaly was never "fast state bad, slow state good" — both steady states grade B correctly. The defect is transition-straddling windows, and the grade letters are tracking exactly that. Which is precisely what the dynamic warmup fixes: it can't (and shouldn't) pick the machine's state, it just refuses to measure until the state stops moving — turning every quick-2-style F into a slightly-delayed B.

This suggests the assertion should also catch your 0,0 evidence (quick-2's F is a reproduction even when the medians survive). I'll add a second criterion: at most one run per cadence below B — your 0,0 quick legs (F + C) fail it, the post-fix expectation (transitions absorbed, occasional ambient C) passes it:

Your quick-leg interpretation is exactly right: one transition window (F), then steady-fast B's.

The waited-leg "odd" case isn't actually contradictory — it's two different instruments disagreeing about two different things. `loop/iter` is a *floor/slope* estimate, deliberately robust: brief noise can't move it, so it reads a steady 0.445 all five runs. But the letter is the **worst of several census-style signals** — disturbed %, dirty-window %, repeat, drift — and those *count contamination events* rather than estimate the constant. A short burst of ambient activity (IRQ burst, background task, my session breathing) during one 600 ms window trips `dirty win` or `repeat` past a threshold and stamps a C, while leaving the floor untouched. That's by design: "how precise is the constant" and "how clean was the room" are different questions, and the letter answers the second. The A→C→B wobble on an unpinned 3900X with a desktop and a bot session is the same C–D ambient range the 0.22 close-out validation recorded all day on this box.

The annoyance is that the test's table doesn't show *which* signal caused the C — it only captures letter and loop/iter. The report line has the answer in parentheses (`disturbed …, dirty win …, drift …, repeat …`); let me carry that through to the table so future oddities explain themselves:

Sharp reading — and quick-2 is the perfect specimen: `drift 0.55%` (the bracket's endpoints both landed *after* the transition) but `repeat ±5.46 ns` (the two calibration attempts straddled it). Repeat and drift are the same detector at two timescales: drift catches a shift *within* one attempt's window, repeat catches one *between* attempts. Your F/D runs will always light up at least one of them, depending on where the transition happened to fall.

On per-column grades: the machinery already does this internally — the letter is computed as the *worst of the individually-scored signals* — it just discards the per-signal scores before printing. So what you're proposing is pure display: show each signal's own letter next to its value, something like

```
environment D  (disturbed 0.45% B, dirty win 12% B, drift 0.55% A, repeat ±5.46 D)
```

and the composite instantly explains itself: no threshold tables in your head, the worst-signal rule visible on the line, and correlations like the one you just spotted become readable at a glance instead of inferred across runs. Cost is near zero since the scores already exist. So yes — with the usual timing caveat: the calibrate block that prints this dies at -2, and the grade machinery is being rebuilt on batch data at -4. This belongs in the rebuilt gauge, not retrofitted into the deleted one. It also slots straight into the machine-readable-output Todo's schema (each signal: value + grade).

216	/// Environment-grade thresholds, one array per signal: the
217	/// ascending cutoffs a signal crosses to score B, C, D, F (below
218	/// the first is A). The overall letter is the worst signal.
219	///
220	/// - **Provisional** — seeded from quiet-3900X spread on
221	///   2026-07-25; the -5 validation pass on both boxes is meant
222	///   to tune them. The design constraint: a quiet release-build
223	///   machine should essentially never leave A/B, because a
224	///   false alarm every third run destroys trust in the warning.
225	/// - WARNINGs print only at D or worse; C is visible in the
226	///   always-printed grade line without shouting. First
227	///   measurements: a quiet 3900X graded B (debug included), a
228	///   restless one C, and a cross-attempt frequency-regime shift
229	///   D with its warning — the intended spread.
230	pub mod grade_thresholds {
231	    /// Disturbed-sample fraction (worst of d_low / d_high).
232	    pub const DISTURBED: [f64; 4] = [0.005, 0.02, 0.05, 0.15];
233	    /// Dirty-window fraction (worst of d_low / d_high).
234	    pub const DIRTY_WINDOWS: [f64; 4] = [0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90];
235	    /// Loop-only floor drift across the calibration bracket.
236	    pub const DRIFT: [f64; 4] = [0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10];
237	    /// Worst relative residual of a ladder point vs the line.
238	    pub const RESID: [f64; 4] = [0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10];
239	    /// Loop-only vs dithered-fit slope divergence.
240	    pub const CROSS: [f64; 4] = [0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20];
241	    /// Worst relative constant change between clean attempts.
242	    pub const REPEAT: [f64; 4] = [0.025, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20];
243	}
244	
245	/// Score one signal against its [`grade_thresholds`] array:
246	/// 0 (A) through 4 (F) — the count of cutoffs crossed.
247	fn grade_score(x: f64, cutoffs: [f64; 4]) -> u8 {
248	    cutoffs.iter().filter(|&&c| x > c).count() as u8
249	}
250	
251	/// The environment grade: the always-printed synthesis of the
252	/// calibration self-checks. Signals are facts about the run;
253	/// `letter` is the worst signal's grade ('F' outright when the
254	/// published attempt carries physical violations).
255	///
256	/// - See notes/chores/chores-04.md#replanning-slope-dither-and-self-checks
257	///   for the design: every check runs every time, a passing
258	///   check is silent, and the one always-visible line carries
259	///   the letter plus the evidence behind it.
260	#[derive(Debug)]
261	pub struct CalGrade {
262	    /// Fraction of dithered samples above [`DISTURBED_MULT`] x
263	    /// the low-quantile floor (worst of the two points).
264	    pub disturbed_frac: f64,
265	    /// Fraction of dithered windows above [`DIRTY_WINDOW_TOL`]
266	    /// over the minimum window mean (worst of the two points).
267	    pub dirty_window_frac: f64,
268	    /// `|l_end - l_start| / l_start` over the loop-only bracket
269	    /// passes — machine-state drift across the calibration.
270	    pub drift_frac: f64,
271	    /// Worst `|residual| / value` of a ladder point against the
272	    /// Theil-Sen line (median-intercept anchored).
273	    pub max_resid_frac: f64,
274	    /// `|fit_slope - slope| / slope`, dithered two-point fit vs
275	    /// the production loop-only slope.
276	    pub slope_cross_frac: f64,
277	    /// Worst relative constant change between the last two clean
278	    /// attempts; `None` when fewer than two attempts came out
279	    /// clean (scored as C at best).
280	    pub repeat_rel: Option<f64>,
281	    /// Largest absolute change of frame/call or frame/sample
282	    /// between the last two clean attempts, in ns — the headline
283	    /// "constants repeat to ±X ns" number.
284	    pub repeat_ns: Option<f64>,
285	    /// Overall letter, worst signal wins: A, B, C, D, or F.
286	    pub letter: char,
287	}
288	
289	impl CalGrade {
290	    /// Worst per-signal score (0=A .. 4=F), with an unknown
291	    /// repeatability floored at C — if two clean attempts never
292	    /// happened, the environment has already said something.
293	    fn score(&self) -> u8 {
294	        let repeat_score = match self.repeat_rel {
295	            Some(r) => grade_score(r, grade_thresholds::REPEAT),
296	            None => 2,
297	        };
298	        [
299	            grade_score(self.disturbed_frac, grade_thresholds::DISTURBED),
300	            grade_score(self.dirty_window_frac, grade_thresholds::DIRTY_WINDOWS),
301	            grade_score(self.drift_frac, grade_thresholds::DRIFT),
302	            grade_score(self.max_resid_frac, grade_thresholds::RESID),
303	            grade_score(self.slope_cross_frac, grade_thresholds::CROSS),
304	            repeat_score,
305	        ]
306	        .into_iter()
307	        .fold(0, u8::max)
308	    }
309	}
310	
311	/// Map a 0..=4 score to its letter (no 'E': 4 is 'F').
312	fn score_letter(score: u8) -> char {
313	    match score {
314	        0 => 'A',
315	        1 => 'B',
316	        2 => 'C',
317	        3 => 'D',
318	        _ => 'F',
319	    }
320	}
321	
322	/// Xorshift64* PRNG for dither lengths. No external dep; phase
323	/// randomization needs rough uniformity, not statistical rigor.
324	struct XorShift64(u64);

# Chores 05

Continuation of [chores-04](chores-04.md). Records landed work;
conventions in [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions) and
[cycle-protocol.md](../cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

## feat: grade the run from raw batches

Commits: [[1]]

Decided in
[Replanning II](chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run):
the overhead subtraction estimates an ill-defined quantity —
additivity is an approximation on a superscalar CPU, the
constants moved ~10% with frequency regimes, and the correction
cancels in same-harness A/B anyway — while the calibration-time
grade certified a ~1 s window *before* the run: the room, not
the exam. This cycle removes the adjustment machinery and moves
grading onto the run's own time-ordered batch data.

### As-built ladder

- [[1]] 0.23.0-0 `chore: open raw-batch grading cycle`
- [[N]] 0.23.0-1 `feat: micro-probe inner-loop sizing` —
  `pick_inner`'s frame input now comes from a ~1 ms
  micro-probe (low quantile over back-to-back timer pairs)
  instead of `cfg.overhead.frame_call_ns`; sizing no longer
  depends on startup calibration. Also lands
  `tests/settle_anomaly.rs`, the `#[ignore]`d settle-anomaly
  acceptance test for the dynamic-warmup Todo — captured
  while the failing baseline (calibrate letter) still exists

Prediction confirmed, and emphatically: ten runs, ten A's, `loop/iter 0.368` identical to three decimals across every one, repeat as tight as ±0.00 ns. The 7600x is a single-state machine under this test — no gearbox, nothing for cadence to catch. (Notably it's also just *faster* here: 0.368 vs the 3900X's 0.438/0.489 — a per-machine constant, not a state.)

That gives the acceptance test its complete cross-machine story, and each box a distinct job:

- **3900X** — the box that exercises the fix: bistable, reproducibly fails today, must go green when warm-until-stable lands.
- **7600x** — the box that guards the *other* promise: "a warm box exits near-immediately." Post-fix, this same all-A table must not change, and the run shouldn't get measurably slower — if the convergence loop ever burns visible time on a machine this steady, that's a regression the 7600x will catch and the 3900X can't.

Recording the vacuous-pass baseline in the acceptance bullet so the close-out validation knows both boxes' expected behavior:

content.text:
Your contention matches the data, and the explanation is the deliciously ironic one: **the first leg is performing unpaid warmup for the second.** By the time the waited leg starts, the quick leg's hammering has already forced the transition and parked the box in its steady-fast state — the second leg is enjoying exactly the service the dynamic-warmup fix will provide to *every* run, just delivered accidentally by the test's own structure. (One caveat to "always": the 0/8 run earlier tonight had the waited leg go D,D,D — an 8 s gap on a hot box re-provokes partial settling. But at 0/0, yes — second leg is reliably the better one.)

Which means the two-leg design has outlived its hypothesis. It was built to show *cadence-dependence*; the refined model is *transition-catching*, and for that a single loop is strictly cleaner: run N times at one gap, and whichever run straddles the state change lights up drift/repeat. The two-gap comparison stops earning its complexity — if we ever want to probe a second duty cycle, that's one env-var rerun, and the full cadence *sweep* belongs to the future selftest command anyway. So: agreed, one loop of 10. Implementing:

Ladder reordered and the Ideas entry updated to record its partial promotion (the fuller cadence-sweep mode stays there for later).

So to answer the question directly: the sub-command lands at -4, and *nothing* is ever lost — calibrate survives until -5, by which point the gauge (-3) and `selftest` (-4) are alive and the acceptance test has already migrated onto them. As a bonus, the -3 overlap window lets us run both grading systems side by side on the same box before trusting the new one — a validation opportunity the original ladder order didn't have.

Currently uncommitted: the single-loop test simplification, the knobs banner, and this replan — they'll ride with the -2 push (batch pipeline) unless you want them landed sooner so the 7600x can pull the simplified test. Next work when you're ready: -2, the time-ordered batch pipeline.

content.text:
Yes — permanently. Its role just refines at each rung:

- **Now → -3**: as-is, parsing the calibrate environment line; keeps failing on the 3900X (the armed baseline).
- **-4**: migrates — its orchestration (spawn N, cadence, per-run parse, verdict logic) moves into `iiac-perf selftest`, and the test shrinks to: run `selftest`, assert the verdict. Same name, same command to invoke it, much less code. It should still fail here, because the warmup is still fixed-count.
- **-5**: calibrate dies; the test doesn't notice — it's on the gauge by then.
- **Dynamic-warmup cycle**: the moment of truth — it flips to green on the 3900X, stays green-and-fast on the 7600x, and then lives on indefinitely as the regression guard for warm-until-stable. If a future change ever breaks convergence, `cargo test --release --test settle_anomaly -- --ignored` is the alarm that rings.

The one knob that keeps mattering across all of it is `IIAC_PERF_BIN` — it's how the test exercises a *saved* binary (like your 0.23.0-1 with its still-parseable calibrate letter) independent of what's in the tree. So: the file survives, the invocation survives, and the failing baseline stays reproducible right up until the fix earns the green.

**-2 is done and ready to commit.** Summary of the working copy:

- `src/harness.rs`: the `BatchPipeline` — samples land in a raw buffer, flushed at 65,536 samples or 50 ms (whichever first, time checked once per 1,024 pushes); each flush computes a `BatchSummary` (floor, mean, max, census over-floor count using the calibration disturbed definition, start/end timestamps) and bulk-records into the histogram; memory bounded at one 512 KiB buffer plus summaries. Blocked mode flushes at block boundaries so no batch spans a sleep gap. Run outputs folded into a new `RunOutput` struct — retiring `print_report`'s standing `too_many_arguments` IOU — and the report header now shows `batches=N`. Three new unit tests cover flush cadence, census counting, and the empty-flush clock move.
- `src/benches/*.rs` (all 14): mechanical conversion to the `RunOutput` API — each is now two clean lines instead of a 6-tuple destructure plus 9-line call.
- Version 0.23.0-2; chores rung appended; -1 refs backfilled (`[[68]]`/`[[2]]`, SHA `769067779b20…`).

Live verification: `min-now -d 2` produced 93 batches (~21 ms each, buffer-full flushes as designed for fast benches); `--blocks 5` prints its full report with block stats intact. One design note for your review: the `BatchSummary` fields carry an `#[allow(dead_code)]` until the -3 gauge becomes their reader — flagged per the convention since it rode in on a larger diff.

Also riding from earlier: the single-loop settle test, its knobs banner, and the ladder reorder (build-then-demolish). Want the commit description draft?
